It's a nifty idea, but here's the obligatory killjoy information security bucket of cold water.

The most secure way to do what you are suggesting would be iframes with sanitized tag attributes, but even those only protect against certain kinds of attacks. Allowing someone to place arbitrary javascript+html, even if it has no way to enumerate voat javascript data, still allows for things like CSRF attacks, tracking, browser PDF vulnerability exploits, etc.

The problem with this is not that these attacks will work everywhere; but they will work on some users and some user's browsers, and almost always without requiring a subreddit visitor to even use the app. The problem is that people are not security literate. It would be nice if they were, but they 99% aren't and will never be.

When someone who is security illiterate goes on a big website, they generally trust that that website isn't going to

  • lead their computer to execute arbitrary out-of-browser code (e.g. install spyware or adware) or allow a stranger to do so.
  • try to commit identity theft on them, or allow any stranger (who happens to be a moderator) on that website to try and do the same.
  • allow any stranger (who happens to be a moderator) on that website to find where they live (IP geolocation) or other information about them (what threads they visit, etc).

Voat right now does not do these things. This is a good thing.

Again, the key thing to keep in mind here is that 99% of people don't know about and don't think about the security risks they take by visiting each page of a particular website; all they really know to do (incorrect as it sometimes is) is to expect that when they go on a big site, it will not hurt them. That the owners of a big site will take care of it so they don't get any of that "malware thing" google is always warning them about.

The subject I was talking about in my above comment is frequently called Web Application Security - the "application" in the name doesn't refer to the specific idea discussed here of embedding apps within web sites, just think of it is as a synonym for "website," though it can also refer to a particular section of a site that acts a lot like a mobile or desktop app.

You can get a professional-side jargon-heavy look at web app security, both general concepts and practical implementation, by going to the OWASP website or searching website security or web app security on youtube.

The best way to learn about security if you are interested into going into it as a career is to learn a little bit about how networking and the internet works, read up about what php and javascript do, learn the concepts of "backend" and "frontend" web development and what their different roles are, and then when you start reading that stuff on OWASP it'll make more sense to you.

It's very easy to get overwhelmed with this stuff. The best way is to smart small. If you are interested in at some point pursuing it professionally, I suggest focus on backend development as there's less competition.

You don't have to commit anything, just see if you can make a php script that will output a webpage with no style or content except the current time. Then maybe the next step would be to see if you can make it so after 5pm the background is black and the text is white.
